You must cite AI code even after editing it, and say whether it is verbatim or modified.
You must cite AI code only when it is nontrivial.
You must list AI-written lines in the README.

student|course|require|during-work.label: Check AI output before you rely on it

items.directive: You must verify and critically evaluate AI output before using it.
You must test, run and debug AI-generated code yourself.
You should not rely on AI output and must review and cite the actual sources.

student|course|require|during-work.label: Submit your AI prompts and transcripts

items.directive: You must include the prompts you used with AI tools, in a file, README, comments, or the hand-in.
You must submit the full conversation, transcript, or session record of your AI interactions.
You must keep complete records of your AI interactions for possible review, and you are encouraged to use a logging tool.
You must submit each AI session report within 24 hours of the conversation.

student|course|require|during-work.label: Write a reflection on how you used AI

items.directive: You must explain how you used AI, how you modified its output, challenges you faced and what you learned.
You must fill out the AI reflection form to receive credit for each assignment where you used AI.
You must submit the AI usage reflection form by the day after submitting the work.
You must submit the explanation of AI use as a separate document with the project.
You must disclose how you validated and revised AI output.

student|course|require|during-work.label: Use required AI tools and follow course procedures
student|course|require|during-work.old_label: Required AI use and course procedures

items.directive: You are expected to use AI coding agents on projects, which are built around the agent writing the code.
You must understand and follow the AI policy of every course you take; policies differ by course.
You should start every AI session with the course-provided tutor prompt.
Do exercises in class on your own keyboard, and make-up sessions follow the same rules.
You must complete homework alongside the course's AI tutor.
You must read an AI academic paper and present it to the class.

student|course|require|during-assessment.label: Show and attest your work during assessments

items.directive: You must discuss your AI use during the demo with the TA.
You must attest that quizzes are completed without AI assistance.
You must record your screen during quizzes.
You must demonstrate your progress to the teaching staff at the end of the assignment.
You should read the department's supplemental academic integrity policy.

student|course|none|during-work.label: Ask before using AI when unsure

items.directive: You should ask staff when you are unsure whether an AI use or tool is allowed.

student|course|none|during-work.label: Use AI cautiously and keep practicing yourself
student|course|none|during-work.old_label: Being cautious about relying on AI

items.directive: You should be cautious with AI and understand its limitations.
You must spend time practicing and take responsibility for learning from the work.
Course materials and instructor guidance take precedence over AI output.
You should not rely on AI tools, because exams are closed-book.
You should consider carefully how showing AI-produced work affects how employers see you.

student|course|none|during-work.label: Cite and disclose your AI use

items.directive: You are not required to submit a form or note when you did not use AI.
You may change flagged parts of your work and resubmit as necessary.

student|course|none|over-time.label: Give feedback on the AI policy

items.directive: You may tell staff if the AI policy disallows something that should be allowed.

P22.03.directive: Do not use unauthorized notes, devices or outside resources during an exam; doing so is cheating.
P22.03.why: Sources (CUNY) list 'Unauthorized use during an examination of notes, prepared answers, or any electronic devices' with no mention of AI; a standard cheating definition restated in an AI document.

P111.09.directive: Include a statement with your work, such as an integrity statement, a note that your instructor permitted GenAI use on the assignment, or a statement that you take responsibility for the work's accuracy and originality.
P111.09.why: Colorado Denver source: 'I have been permitted, by my faculty member, to use GenAI on this assignment'; Yeshiva: 'take responsibility for the accuracy and originality'.

P16.10.directive: Write code comments in your own words.
P16.10.why: Dartmouth source says only 'All comments should be your own words.' with no AI reference.

P93.03.directive: Refine and revise your prompts to AI tools through repeated rounds, and do not expect the best result on the first try.
P93.03.why: Sources are about prompting AI: 'refine your prompts', 'engineer your prompt', 'iterating with the tool as you work'.

P93.05.directive: Write clear, specific and detailed prompts to AI tools that give context, and avoid vague, minimal prompts.
P93.05.why: Sources are about prompts: 'Good prompts include clear directions', 'improve a GenAI system's understanding of your queries'.

P93.07.directive: When prompting AI, break complex tasks into parts, set context in your first prompt, and ask follow-up questions or for multiple versions.
P93.07.why: Duke source: 'Use your first prompt to set the context for the chat'; others: 'Ask follow-up questions', 'Ask for multiple versions'.

P125.02.directive: Perform due diligence on your work before submitting it.
P125.02.why: Oregon State source: 'students perform due diligence' with no AI reference.

P40.06.directive: Write your work in Google Docs or Office 365 so editing history can be viewed.
P40.06.why: Sources ask students to use Office 365 or compose 'in Google Docs' and mention plagiarism and citations, but none mentions AI.

P115.16.directive: Review the academic integrity policy or contact the named office with questions.
P115.16.why: Sources point to integrity resources and offices ('contact the Office of Academic Standards', 'Academic Integrity resources'); only Gonzaga mentions AI, so this is a general procedural pointer.

P26.10.directive: Keep drafts, notes and version histories as evidence of your own work process, such as proof that AI was not used or of how you transformed or curated AI outputs.
P26.10.why: Clemson: 'retain records of their original work as proof that AI was not used'; Minnesota: 'how they have transformed or curated AI outputs'.

P99.10.directive: Give yourself enough time to complete your work to avoid academic integrity violations.
P99.10.why: Yeshiva source: 'giving yourself the time needed to complete your work will help you avoid academic integrity' violations; no AI reference.

P119.04.directive: Personalize and customize your application materials to stand out.
P119.04.why: George Mason source: 'Set yourself apart by personalizing and customizing your materials.'; general career advice with no AI reference.

P81.15.directive: You may receive informal violations, which are not stored in the university database, and formal ones, which are.
P81.15.why: Michigan-Dearborn sources describe informal and formal violations stored in the university database; a general integrity procedure.

P127.08.directive: If you work in a group, all students in the group are held equally responsible for a violation.
P127.08.why: Washington source: 'all students will be held equally responsible for violation'; a general group-work integrity rule.

P64.07.directive: You must submit your written statement within the set deadline after an allegation.
P64.07.why: Grinnell source: 'the statement must be submitted within 3 business days'; a general allegation-procedure deadline.

CT17.c06.directive: You must produce the work you submit yourself; graded code must be written without assistance from AI, and AI tools may not take the place of developing your own solution.
CT17.c06.why: Drexel: 'written by the student without assistance from AI'; Harvey Mudd: 'they may not be used in place of developing a solution' (they = the AI tools).

CT32.c05.directive: You must write your own code and must not copy, share, or submit code you did not write, including code from homework help sites, a TA or generative AI.
CT32.c05.why: Michigan State: 'never submit a code that is not yours even if you received that code from a TA or from any Generative AI'; Memphis names 'homework help' sites.

CT15.c04.directive: You must not use code fragments found through search directly in your solutions.
CT15.c04.why: Wellesley source: 'fragments, you are not allowed to use these directly in your solutions'; about search results, no AI reference.

CT22.c05.directive: You may not upload any files or images to the university's Gemini AI tool.
CT22.c05.why: NC State source: 'No files (or images) are allowed to be uploaded to NCSU Gemini.' Gemini is an AI tool.

CT12.c04.directive: You must not use AI or other writing aids, such as Grammarly, predictive text or translation tools, that revise your sentences or clean up your English.
CT12.c04.why: BYU-Idaho: 'Use AI to clean up your English.' (listed as not allowed); North Texas names Grammarly, predictive text and translation tools; Pomona: 'tools that offer suggested revisions of your sentences'.

CT27.c04.directive: You must not edit, truncate, tamper with, scrub, or regenerate your AI prompts, responses, transcripts or session logs, and you must attest they are complete.
CT27.c04.why: NC State: 'prompts and responses must not be edited or truncated'; UIUC: 'tampering with Claude Code session logs', 'Never ask the AI to reproduce the conversation'.

CT27.c05.directive: Links to AI logs are not accepted as submitted AI transcripts.
CT27.c05.why: Columbia source: 'links to logs are not accepted.' in the context of submitting AI interaction logs.

CT35.c14.directive: You must submit homework as scans of handwritten originals.
CT35.c14.why: Stony Brook source: 'All homework assignments must be submitted as scans of handwritten originals.'; no AI reference.

CT35.c10.directive: If your test answer can be found on the internet, you receive a zero for the test.
CT35.c10.why: Georgia Southern source: 'If your answer to a question can be found on the internet, then your score for the test is zero.'; no AI reference.

CT35.c11.directive: You must not use an IDE on exams and are restricted to a terminal editor.
CT35.c11.why: Rose-Hulman source: 'refrain from using an IDE, and are restricted to' a terminal editor; no AI reference.

CT21.c04.directive: If you have significant programming experience and are working on comprehensive projects, you may generally use AI coding agents.
CT21.c04.why: Loyola Marymount: 'agentic coding is generally acceptable' for experienced students on comprehensive projects; agentic coding is AI coding agents.

CT21.c06.directive: You may set an AI coding agent up on a long task and walk away.
CT21.c06.why: UIUC source: 'setting your agent up on a long task and walking away', in a course built on Claude Code agents.

CT46.c06.directive: You must purchase a Claude Pro AI subscription for the project and should expect two to three months of cost.
CT46.c06.why: UIUC: 'purchase a Claude Pro subscription'; Claude is an AI tool.

CT30.c02.directive: You must understand and be able to explain all code you submit, including everything AI tools suggest; do not copy code you do not understand.
CT30.c02.why: Brown: 'replicate it on your own, without collaboration or AI assistance'; Bucknell: 'Never blindly copy code! You MUST understand everything these tools suggest.'

CT30.c08.directive: You must comment your code to show you understand it and what it does.
CT30.c08.why: Maryland: 'explain the output of any code and comment it'; Texas Tyler: 'Comment on each line of code in the imported method'; neither mentions AI.

CT27.c01.directive: You must include the prompts you used with AI tools, in a file, README, comments, or the hand-in.
CT27.c01.why: Carleton: 'the name and version of the specific LLM you used, as well as the exact prompts'; Brown: 'link to the conversation history or a list of the prompts used'.

CT35.c12.directive: Do exercises in class on your own keyboard, and make-up sessions follow the same rules.
CT35.c12.why: San Francisco source: 'Exercises are done in the room, during the session, on your own keyboard.'; no AI reference.

CT35.c03.directive: You must record your screen during quizzes.
CT35.c03.why: Duke source: 'be asked to record your screen'; no AI reference.

CT35.c17.directive: You must demonstrate your progress to the teaching staff at the end of the assignment.
CT35.c17.why: WPI source: 'demonstrate their progress to the teaching staff at the conclusion of the assignment'; no AI reference.

CT48.c04.directive: You should read the department's supplemental academic integrity policy.
CT48.c04.why: Villanova source: 'review the supplemental academic integrity policy from the computing science department'; no AI reference.

CT40.c12.directive: You must spend time practicing and take responsibility for learning from the work.
CT40.c12.why: UMBC: 'responsibility to learn from this process'; Temple: 'spend time practicing problem solving and writing'; neither mentions AI.

OTHER.c27.directive: You may change flagged parts of your work and resubmit as necessary.
OTHER.c27.why: Washington State source: 'you'll be able to change them and resubmit as necessary'; no AI reference.

CT06.c07.directive: You may tell staff if the AI policy disallows something that should be allowed.
CT06.c07.why: Washington source: 'If you believe the policy disallows something that should be allowed' appears in the course AI policy, so 'the policy' is the AI policy.
